sections.h2: Who sends and collects property tax bills
sections.html:
The county collector of revenue bills and collects, and the assessor values the land. Doug Trentmann is the Franklin County Collector, in Room 103 at 400 E Locust in Union, phone 636-583-6353. His office handles current and delinquent taxes for the county and 64 other taxing entities, plus levee, railroad and utility taxes and merchant and manufacturer licenses.

There are four ways to pay:

  • Online through the Property Tax Bill Pay page on the county website
  • By phone at 877-690-3729 with jurisdiction code 3570
  • In the Collector's office with a check or cash
  • By mailing a check to the address on the bill

A nominal convenience fee is charged on these services.

The assessor does not figure taxes, set rates or print bills. Each taxing jurisdiction sets its own levy, so rate questions go to those bodies and their annual budget meetings.

sections.h2: Franklin County housing at a glance
sections.html:
Franklin County is a large exurban county on the south side of the Missouri River, part of the St. Louis metro area, with Union as the county seat. Population is 108,090, up 3.3 percent from the 2020 base. There are 48,091 housing units, and 76.5 percent of occupied homes are lived in by their owners. The typical owner-occupied value is $227,600, and 794 building permits were issued in 2025.

Incorporated places are Berger, Gerald, New Haven, Pacific, St. Clair, Sullivan, Union and Washington. A seller inside a city pays a city bill too, so a Washington or Pacific address means two sets of statements.

The assessor tracks more than 73,000 parcels, roughly 50,000 of them residential, 24,000 agricultural and 3,400 commercial. The office reassesses all real estate every two years and mails more than 20,000 value-increase notices a year.

Statute fixes the percentages. The residential ratio in RSMo 137.115 is 19 percent of true value, and farm and commercial parcels use their own percentages. Raising a house more than 15 percent without new building requires an on-site inspection first.

The assessor also fields requests from title companies and mortgage lenders, and the county's property search site lets an owner pull up the parcel record before calling. Check the acreage, square footage and bedroom count on the record, since errors there change the value.

The assessor publishes a yearly calendar that shows where a house stands in the cycle.

Franklin County assessment and billing calendar
DateWhat happens
January 1Valuation date for all real and personal property
March 1Personal property list due, with penalties if late
June 30Real estate and personal property rolls go to the County Clerk
Second Monday in JulyLast day to file a Board of Equalization appeal
September 30State Tax Commission deadline, or later if the Board's letter came within the last month
October 1Tax rates set and certified to the County Clerk
November and DecemberCollector prepares and sends bills
December 31Current taxes must be paid before they become delinquent

Utilities and railroads report to the assessor by April 1, and the clerk certifies those values by April 20.

Begin with the assessor's staff. They hold many informal hearings, mostly in reassessment years, and try to settle concerns before they turn into Board filings. Ask which sales the value leans on, then line them up against houses on your own street.

The formal step is the Board of Equalization, with the July deadline shown in the calendar above. Assessor staff present the facts to the Board. A value that jumped 15 percent or more for reasons other than new building puts the burden on the assessor under RSMo 138.060.

After the Board, the State Tax Commission is the next level, and the county's attorney represents the assessor in that case. A claim that a property should be exempt altogether goes to circuit court instead. Owners that are LLCs, trusts, estates or corporations need a lawyer to file.

sections.h2: Relief for seniors and disabled owners
sections.html:
Missouri does not exempt the property of seniors or disabled owners. The state instead offers the Missouri Property Tax Credit, which gives income-limited seniors and disabled residents a refund or income tax credit based on property tax or rent paid. Details are at the state Department of Revenue site, and Aging Ahead answers questions at 636-629-3143.

The Homestead Preservation Act credit needs a legislative appropriation and is not funded at this time.

sections.h2: If taxes go unpaid past December 31
sections.html:
A bill left open after December 31 becomes delinquent and draws penalties. The statutory penalty is 18 percent of that year's delinquency (RSMo 140.100), and the postmark decides whether a mailed check was on time.

Owners who dispute a value can still pay in full and file a protest statement with the collector, then sue the collector inside 90 days, as RSMo 139.031 requires. That same section allows a credit or refund for tax paid by mistake when the application comes within three years.

Land with old unpaid years goes into the county's annual August tax sale. Owners can redeem at any point before it by paying the tax, penalty and costs. The Collector can give the figure for a specific parcel at 636-583-6353.

sections.h2: Handling property tax when you sell
sections.html:
Pull the parcel from the pay site and print the current bill, then ask the Collector at 636-583-6353 whether any earlier year is open. The title company will need the parcel ID and the payoff figure. The sales contract decides who owes which part of the current year, so have the title company read that clause before closing.

If the house is inherited, behind on taxes or has tenants or repairs outstanding, a cash purchase can pay the tax balance at the closing table, out of the price. Franklin County deeds are filed at the Recorder of Deeds, and the county website has a Record My Deeds link on its home page. A cash sale skips the lender's appraisal and the repair requests that often come with it.

faqs.q: Where do I pay Franklin County property tax?
faqs.a: At the Collector's office, Room 103, 400 E Locust in Union, or online, by phone at 877-690-3729 with code 3570, or by mail. A nominal convenience fee applies to these services.

faqs.q: When is the Franklin County tax deadline?
faqs.a: December 31. After that date current taxes are delinquent and penalties are applied.

faqs.q: How do I contest a Franklin County assessment?
faqs.a: Call the assessor, then file with the Board of Equalization by the second Monday in July. If the Board does not change the value, the State Tax Commission is the next stop.

faqs.q: How often does Franklin County reassess homes?
faqs.a: Every two years. New construction gets assessed every year, and the county mails more than 20,000 notices of increased value annually.

faqs.q: Is there property tax relief for Franklin County seniors?
faqs.a: There is a state refund and credit. The Missouri Property Tax Credit helps seniors and disabled residents with limited income. The Homestead Preservation Act credit is not funded now.
